ctx.x: The Tree of Hope was just in front of the entrance to Connie's Inn. It was said that when you touched the tree and made a wish, you would have your hopes come true. That was a superstition mostly among theatrical people but there was seldom a time if a musician passed the tree that he would not touch it to bring him luck whether he w as superstitious or not. How long this legendary tree had been there I do not know, but I became one of those who touched it every time I passed it and most of the time I had no…

When I came to New York and long before that, I was known as Johnson Coleman and sometimes people call others by their last names only. So some called me Johnson, and others called me Coleman which made some people think that my name was Coleman Johnson. And some of the hoppers at the "Track" knew the names of most of our group but they were not certain as who was who and I've had many of them calling me Dickie and they would call Dickie Wells, Coleman, when they saw us on the streets and we were not together.

August 1928 came and we went on a tour. We had been in the Savoy for six months, the longest run the band had ever had in the same place. Our first stop was Pittsburgh and we left New York on a Greyhound bus in the early afternoon and stopped in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania where I got the surprise of my life. This was a regular Greyhound stop at a restaurant where the buses were timed from their starting point to stop during the lunch or supper hour.
